facts.title: Two envoys and a distorted death
facts.body: Holbein painted The Ambassadors in 1533. The National Gallery identifies Jean de Dinteville, French ambassador to England, and Georges de Selve, bishop and envoy. Between them stretches a shelf of worldly learning — and a skull you can only read from the side.

facts.title: Dinteville in silk and dagger
facts.body: Jean de Dinteville, left, wears the luxurious stillness of a court diplomat. Holbein catalogs status through fabrics and a sheathed dagger while the man’s gaze holds you at interview distance.

facts.title: Selve in clerical gravity
facts.body: Georges de Selve, right, balances secular pomp with episcopal restraint. Together the pair embody church and state negotiating a fractured Europe — Reformation politics folded into friendship.

facts.title: Death, stretched across the floor
facts.body: The famous anamorphic skull only resolves when viewed from an extreme angle. Holbein plants memento mori inside diplomatic display: approach knowledge, then remember you are temporary.

facts.title: Stars on the upper shelf
facts.body: A celestial globe sits among the upper instruments — the heavens made portable. Ambassadors claim not only countries, but the sky’s measurable order.

facts.title: Time caught in brass
facts.body: Dials and sundials advertise precision timekeeping. In 1533, mastering hours was political power as much as science.

facts.title: A quadrant for the heavens
facts.body: The quadrant belongs to the toolkit of astronomy and navigation. Holbein paints expertise as still life — knowledge you could almost adjust.

facts.title: A world you can spin
facts.body: The terrestrial globe advertises geographic mastery — the ambassadors’ century inventing itself as a measurable planet. Empire and curiosity share the same polished sphere.

facts.title: A string that will not play
facts.body: A lute with a broken string sits among the instruments — often read as discord in the Church or the limits of earthly harmony. Music, like diplomacy, can go out of tune.

facts.title: Flutes in their case
facts.body: A case of flutes continues the musical theme. Harmony is collected, catalogued — and still vulnerable to a single broken course on the lute beside it.

facts.title: Open pages of Reform
facts.body: An open hymnal has been linked to Lutheran music — doctrine entering through song. Even the still life argues about Europe’s religious fracture.

facts.title: Numbers for merchants and minds
facts.body: A book of arithmetic grounds the lower shelf in practical calculation. Diplomacy runs on ledgers as much as on Latin.

facts.title: Christ half hidden by the curtain
facts.body: A silver crucifix peeks from behind the green curtain at upper left. Faith remains in the room, but edged to the margin — a quiet counterweight to instruments and skull.

facts.title: The curtain of state
facts.body: The rich green drape stages the envoys like a court backdrop. Holbein’s theater of diplomacy needs fabric as much as faces.

facts.title: Steel at the hip
facts.body: Dinteville’s dagger is ornament and threat in one sheath. Soft power still keeps a blade within reach.

facts.title: Cosmati geometry underfoot
facts.body: The pavement echoes Cosmati work associated with Westminster Abbey. Sacred geometry grounds the envoys — England’s great church literally under diplomatic feet.

facts.title: Shelf of the sciences
facts.body: Upper and lower shelves stack into a curriculum of astronomy, geometry, music, and measurement. Holbein paints the Renaissance mind as furniture between two living men.
